A1.notes.Q3: Privacy is key. Sensitive data needs a very strong justification. Focusing on factors related to academic *engagement* seems less intrusive.
A1.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for advisors to trust the model & provide effective support. Big accuracy gains aren't useful if we can’t understand *why*.
A1.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount. A slightly less accurate model that helps all students equally is preferable to one which exacerbates existing inequalities.
A1.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is best, but needs resources. Frequent check-ins are good, avoid overwhelming students.
A1.notes.Q7: For generic alerts, a wider net is okay; for personalized outreach, accuracy/precision becomes more important to respect student time.
A1.Q8.1: The model should be continually monitored for unintended bias and adjusted accordingly. Data drift could also be an issue over time.

A2.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, but some data adds value if used responsibly. I'm hesitant about demographic data unless it demonstrably improves fairness. Absalon data needs careful consideration.
A2.notes.Q4: Explainability is key for building trust with students and justifying interventions. A 'black box' model won’t work in practice, even if more accurate.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount; we can't perpetuate existing inequalities. A slight decrease in overall identification is acceptable to ensure equitable support access.
A2.notes.Q6: Personalized contact and an open invitation for discussion are most helpful. Frequent, generic emails will be ignored.
A2.notes.Q7: With a simple email, reaching more students is okay; with personalized outreach, fewer false positives are important as it takes advisor time.
A2.Q8.1: The survey doesn’t address data security beyond privacy laws. We need to be confident in how the university protects this information from breaches.

A3.notes.Q3: It's a slippery slope with sensitive data, even if there is an improvement. We need to be *very* cautious and prioritize student wellbeing over model accuracy.
A3.notes.Q4: Explainability is key for advisors to be able to trust and act on the model's output. Losing *too* much explainability makes it unusable in practice.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial; we can’t exacerbate existing inequalities. A slight dip in overall accuracy to ensure equitable outcomes is acceptable and responsible.
A3.notes.Q6: Personalized communication builds trust & allows for nuanced support. Invitation to a meeting is good, too. Twice yearly feels frequent enough without being overwhelming.
A3.notes.Q7: Generic emails are fine for initial contact but require more careful selection criteria. More targeted interventions warrant a bit more selective approach to avoid overburdening the system and advisors.
A3.Q8.1: The survey doesn't address how often we *re-evaluate* the model's fairness or accuracy after implementation. This is crucial!

S1.notes.Q3: I’m wary of data collection, having dropped out before. Financial situation & first-gen status feel more directly linked to support needs, so okay with small improvements there.
S1.notes.Q4: Explainability is *crucial*. If I don't understand why a system flags me, it’s useless and could increase anxiety. High/Moderate is ok, anything less isn't.
S1.notes.Q5: Fairness *has* to be a priority, even if it means fewer students are reached overall. Missing vulnerable groups is unacceptable. I want recall across groups prioritized.
S1.notes.Q6: A personalized email feels less intrusive, but a follow-up meeting option is good. Constant contact would be overwhelming.
S1.notes.Q7: Personalized outreach needs to be more targeted; contacting lots of people with detailed info feels intrusive if it’s not needed. General emails can cope with wider reach.
S1.Q8.1: I'm concerned about the potential for this model to reinforce existing biases and unfairly target students who are already struggling, even unintentionally. Real support systems need human connection.

S2.notes.Q3: I'm wary of data collection, especially anything too personal. Some data is fine if it truly helps, but privacy needs strong protection. Nationality feels a bit sensitive.
S2.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for trust and to allow advisors to properly help students. A black box isn't helpful; we need to understand *why* someone's flagged.
S2.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital, but some loss of overall identification seems acceptable if it means equitable support. Missing a few students is better than systematically disadvantaging groups.
S2.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is important; a generic email feels impersonal. An invitation to chat with an advisor seems most useful, but not constantly.
S2.notes.Q7: For simple notifications, contacting more students is okay. But for personalized support it's important to avoid overwhelming advisors with false positives.
S2.Q8.1: It would be good to know how the data will be stored and secured long-term, beyond just 'applicable privacy laws'. Data breaches are a real concern.

S3.notes.Q3: Privacy is very important, but disability data *could* be helpful if used to ensure support is tailored and fair. Strong safeguards are critical.
S3.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital, especially given my own experiences navigating support services. The more opaque the model, the less trust there will be.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness should be prioritized even if it means slightly lower overall accuracy. Missing students who need help is bad, but perpetuating inequalities is worse.
S3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels more supportive and less intrusive than generic emails. A meeting allows for nuanced discussion.
S3.notes.Q7: With personalized follow-up, a slightly broader net is okay but I'd prefer fewer false positives in that case.
S3.Q8.1: The survey doesn’t address how the model handles students with chronic health conditions - are accommodations built into the outreach? This needs to be considered.

S4.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, but disability *might* be relevant for targeted support, if used carefully to avoid bias.
S4.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial, especially with my experience. I’d want to understand why a decision was made about *me*. Less accuracy is okay if it means more transparency.
S4.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital! A system making things worse for marginalized students isn’t helpful. I'd rather fewer people get flagged if it helps close equity gaps.
S4.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels less intrusive and more supportive than a generic blast. A meeting is good if I want more help.
S4.notes.Q7: Fewer students contacted with personalized emails, but balancing between reaching enough people and not wasting resources on low-impact contact.
S4.Q8.1: The system needs to be flexible and allow for self-reporting of difficulties. A model can’t capture everything, and student agency is key.

S5.notes.Q3: I’m cautious about privacy, but understand data can help. Nationality & first-gen status seem relevant to adjustment challenges and could benefit from targeted support if fairness improves.
S5.notes.Q4: Explainability is important, especially as an international student still navigating the system. A little less accuracy is worth it if I understand *why* something happened.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount. It wouldn’t be right to perpetuate existing inequalities, even if overall numbers improve slightly. Prioritizing identifying those being missed feels key.
S5.notes.Q6: Personalized support is best, but not intrusive. A meeting *option* allows for in-depth discussion. Twice a year feels like enough without being overwhelming.
S5.notes.Q7: Personalized outreach needs to be more targeted. It's better to contact fewer students meaningfully than many superficially. A broad email is okay if it just shares resources.
S5.Q8.1: It would be helpful to know how the model addresses cultural differences and varying academic backgrounds, especially for international students like myself. The survey did not cover this specifically.

S6.notes.Q3: I'm wary of data collection, especially after dropping out once. National origin and financial aid seem too sensitive unless a strong fairness argument is made.
S6.notes.Q4: Explainability is *really* important, especially for students who might already feel vulnerable about seeking help. I'd accept some accuracy loss for clear explanations.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial, and it’s not right to exacerbate existing inequalities. A small dip in overall identification is worth ensuring everyone has equal access to support.
S6.notes.Q6: A personalized approach feels less intrusive and more supportive than a generic email. I also think regular check-ins would be better.
S6.notes.Q7: The risk of stressing students out with false positives is too high for generalized outreach. Personalized means fewer, but more meaningful interactions.
S6.Q8.1: I'm concerned about the potential for this system to create a self-fulfilling prophecy – labelling someone as ‘at risk’ might unintentionally reinforce those difficulties.

S7.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, especially with sensitive data. Disability info *could* be useful for targeted support but needs careful handling to avoid stigmatization.
S7.notes.Q4: Explainability is key for trust. A model needs to be understandable, and losing that for a small accuracy gain isn’t worth it.
S7.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital. It's unacceptable if the model disproportionately misses students from certain groups, even at a small cost to overall accuracy.
S7.notes.Q6: Personalized support is best, but not overly intrusive. A meeting allows for nuanced discussion; email provides a first step.
S7.notes.Q7: For general info emails, reaching more students is good, even with some false positives. With personalized contact the risk of being wrong is too high.
S7.Q8.1: It's important to consider how a predictive model might interact with existing support services and ensure it doesn’t create another barrier for students needing help.

S8.notes.Q3: Privacy is really important, and the Absalon data feels like a step too far. First-gen status and financial aid might be relevant, but only if it helps address unfairness.
S8.notes.Q4: Explainability is key, especially for me having restarted my studies. I’d want to understand *why* someone flagged me and what I could do about it. Less accuracy isn't worth a black box.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. It’s not okay to perpetuate existing inequalities, even if that means helping fewer students overall. Identifying those who are falling through the cracks in all groups matters most.
S8.notes.Q6: A generic email feels impersonal. Personalized contact or a meeting is much better. Twice a year feels like a good balance – not too often, but enough to be proactive.
S8.notes.Q7: With simple outreach (email), reaching more students seems okay. But with personal contact, accuracy is really important - fewer false positives are vital to maintaining trust.
S8.Q8.1: The survey doesn't ask about *how* the support services will be designed. Are they culturally sensitive? Accessible to students from different backgrounds?

S9.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, especially given my own experiences. But if it helps identify students *before* they reach crisis point, some data sharing could be okay, but sensitivity is crucial.
S9.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital, particularly as someone with a long-term condition impacting my studies. Knowing *why* I was flagged would help me engage constructively.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness is non-negotiable. It’s unacceptable if the system disadvantages already vulnerable groups. A slight drop in overall accuracy is worth it for equitable outcomes.
S9.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels less intrusive and more supportive than a generic email, but it needs to be paired with the option for further discussion.
S9.notes.Q7: I'd rather fewer false positives in personalized outreach, especially since that requires more resources. A balance is good for generic alerts.
S9.Q8.1: The survey doesn’t address the potential for bias in the initial data used to train the model – historical patterns might reflect existing inequalities. Also important: student agency and ability to opt-out.
